summary: Young children (5-6) learn to recognise UK coins (1p, 2p, 5p, 10p, 20p, 50p, £1, £2) and notes (£5, £10, £20, £50) and to know each one's VALUE. The core hurdle is that value is invisible and set by convention, not by physical size, colour, or how many coins there are: a small silver 5p is worth more than a larger bronze 2p, and one £2 coin is worth more than a small heap of pennies (for example, ten 1p coins make only 10p). Activities centre on handling real money and repeatedly asking 'what is it WORTH?' rather than 'how big?' or 'how many?'.
misconceptions: Judges value by physical size or colour (a 2p is bigger than a 5p, so 'worth more')
Thinks more coins means more money (a pile of pennies beats a single £2)
Confuses one penny and one pound
Doesn't recognise notes as money, or treats all notes as the same value

activities.title: Till total: more coins is not always more money
steps: Drop real coins (or coins onto a running-total mat/till) one at a time and watch the TOTAL VALUE build up.
Drop ten 1p coins into the till and read the total (10p); then drop a single £2 coin beside them and see the total leap far higher than the whole heap of pennies.
Say in your own words why one coin can be worth more than many coins.
Run a 'which is worth more?' duel: put a big bronze 2p against a small silver 5p, predict which wins, then reveal/count the values to check.
activities.insight: A set's worth is its total VALUE, not the number of coins or their size; one high-value coin can outweigh many low-value coins, and the smaller coin can be worth more.

activities.title: Order coins on a value line
steps: Handle real coins and sort them, naming each by its value.
Place each coin in order from least worth to most worth along a value line running 1p to £2 (1p, 2p, 5p, 10p, 20p, 50p, £1, £2).
Notice where a physically small coin (5p) sits ahead of a physically bigger coin (2p) on the line.
Answer 'which is worth more?' for pairs you place, giving the value as your reason.
activities.insight: Coins have a fixed order BY VALUE that does not follow their physical size or colour; a 5p comes after a 2p even though it is smaller.

activities.title: Recognise and compare coins and notes
steps: Look at each coin and note and name it and say its value.
Reveal or state a comparison fact for each: 'is this worth more than, less than, or the same as a 10p?'
Introduce notes once coins are secure: name £5, £10, £20, £50 and say which is worth more.
Say that a pound is WORTH a hundred pennies (not 'a hundred times bigger').
activities.insight: Every coin and note can be recognised and matched to a known value, and notes are money too — different notes have different values.

activities.title: Shopkeeper: hand over coins by value
steps: Play a shop where a shopkeeper asks you to hand over a coin by its value ('give me the one worth 5p', 'give me something worth more than a 10p').
Explain out loud why the coin you chose is worth what the shopkeeper asked.
Swap roles so you ask for coins by value too.
activities.insight: You can identify and select coins by their worth, using value rather than appearance to respond.

checkQuestion: Ask the value, THEN the reason: (1) Show a 5p and a 2p: 'Which coin is worth more?' then 'How do you know?' (2) Show ten 1p coins beside one 50p: 'Which is more money?' then 'Why?' (3) 'Which is worth more, a £2 coin or a 50p coin? How do you know?' and 'Point to the £5 note and the £10 note — which is worth more?' Listen to the REASON: a correct child cites the printed value; an incorrect one cites size, colour or how many.
checkAnswer: Says the 5p is worth more than the 2p BECAUSE 5 is more than 2 (its value, not its size); says the single 50p is more money than ten pennies (50 > 10) despite fewer coins; says £2 > 50p and £10 > £5 by their values.
